headline: The 11 PM HRRR dropped its Friday-morning burst, so the dawn showers look light (consensus 0.22 in in 3 hours, about 6 to 9 AM, from RRFS) while the 7.9 ft high tide runs about 1.5 ft high; HRRR's new Saturday 4 PM cell is a lone, low-confidence shower: no street flooding expected.

summary.text: HRRR's 11 PM run dropped the Friday-morning burst (0.33 in down to about 0.04 in). Its wettest 3 hours moved to a lone Saturday 4 to 7 PM cell (0.38 in) no other model supports.
Wettest 3 hours, next 72 h: HRRR 0.38 (Sat), GFS 0.38 (copies HRRR), RRFS 0.22 (Fri), NBM 0.11, ECMWF 0.09. Consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 0.48, RRFS 0.22, NBM 0.11: middle value) 0.22 in.
Most likely nothing beyond full gutters. A stray heavy shower could briefly put water on the sidewalk. Yellow (garage) needs about 0.71 in in 3 hours or a 0.40 in hour.
Showers most likely about 6 to 9 AM Friday, ending by early afternoon. Dry Friday night. Light showers return late Saturday afternoon and evening into Sunday.
Friday's 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM runs about 9.5 ft on NOAA's Bay model (~1.5 ft surge), overlapping the showers. Channel low: Alameda 0.27 ft, Caltrain 0.07 ft.
No need to move cars. A glance at the page between 6 and 10 AM Friday is enough; clear leaves from drain grates in daylight before Tuesday's bigger storm.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Cold, unstable air behind Thursday's low is keeping scattered showers going over the Bay Area tonight, though NWS San Francisco's 11:50 PM discussion notes shower activity has trended down this evening. NWS expects the best chance of showers Friday morning into early afternoon, with a 10% chance of thunderstorms, slightly higher in the late morning and early afternoon. Friday evening into early Saturday turns dry and cold. A weaker system brings light showers to the Bay Area by late Saturday afternoon into Sunday (NWS: a tenth to a quarter inch from Saturday to early Monday), with a warning that saturated soils make nuisance flooding more likely if stronger showers develop. Monday is the dry day. A stronger, negatively tilted trough arrives Tuesday into Wednesday with possible thunderstorms and moderate to heavy rain (NWS: 1 to 1.5 in for most of the Bay Area), together with the king tides of November 24 to 26.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since the 10:25 PM discussion, the HRRR has flipped again. The 11 PM run removes the Friday-morning shower band that the 8 PM run had (0.33 in in its wettest 3 hours, about 5 to 8 AM); its hourly output now shows only 0.04 in in the hour ending 5 AM Friday. Its 15-minute output still has one short cell, 0.11 in in the 15 minutes ending 8:15 AM and 0.13 in in total around 8 AM, but that is a single pop-up shower, not a band.

The HRRR's wettest 3 hours are now Saturday 4 to 7 PM (0.38 in), almost all of it one hour: 0.31 in ending 5 PM. No other model supports it (RRFS has nothing then and only 0.03 in around 8 to 9 PM; NBM and ECMWF are dry or near dry), and GFS shows exactly the same numbers, so it is repeating the HRRR rather than confirming it. I treat it as a low-confidence shower cell, though it lines up with NWS timing for the next weak system.

The independent models keep Friday morning as the wettest stretch. RRFS (4 PM Thu run) has 0.07 in ending 4 AM, 0.15 in ending 7 AM and 0.08 in ending 9 AM: 0.22 in in its wettest 3 hours, 6 to 9 AM. NBM is 0.11 in over the same hours (no hour above 0.05 in). ECMWF is a steady 0.02 to 0.03 in per hour, 0.09 in from 4 to 7 AM.

The dashboard's consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 0.48, RRFS 0.22, NBM 0.11; middle value) is 0.22 in, up slightly from 0.18 in, but the middle value is now the RRFS Friday-morning number rather than a HRRR burst. I think that is a fair figure for Friday morning; the HRRR ×1.25 value comes from the unsupported Saturday cell and probably overstates the risk.

Storm totals for the next 72 hours: GFS 0.53 in, RRFS 0.53, HRRR 0.47 (its run ends Saturday 10 PM), NBM 0.37, ECMWF 0.30.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
NOAA's Bay model still runs well above the predicted tide. After the 1.6 ft low at 2:07 AM (about 3.0 ft on the model, ~1.3 ft high), the water rises through the Friday-morning showers: about 5.3 ft at 5 AM, 6.8 ft at 6 AM, 8.2 ft at 7 AM and 9.2 ft at 8 AM, peaking near 9.5 ft around 9 AM with the 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM, about 1.5 ft of surge. That is the overlap to note, since high Bay water slows the channel's drainage, but with rates this light it should not matter. Friday's 6.4 ft evening high at 9:15 PM runs about 8.1 ft; Saturday's 8.4 ft high at 9:06 AM about 9.8 ft. The HRRR's Saturday 4 to 5 PM cell would fall near the 0.3 ft low at 4:05 PM (about 1.5 ft on the model), the best case for drainage. The model run ends Saturday 7 PM.

The Coastal Flood Advisory for Bayshore locations continues until 11 AM Saturday, with up to 1.8 ft of surge. NWS says it will likely be upgraded to a Coastal Flood Warning on Sunday as the king tides approach.

Channel: at Alameda de las Pulgas the gauge reads 0.27 ft at midnight, steady (Flood Monitoring 3.18 ft). Upstream of Caltrain the last reading is still 0.07 ft at 5:13 PM Thursday (no newer stage reading in the county feed), far below Flood Monitoring (2.8 ft).

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Still a lull on the street. The Caltrain rain gauge's last tip was 0.04 in at 7:01 PM; nothing in the last 3 hours, 0.04 in over 6 hours and 0.44 in over 24 hours. The channel is low and steady.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Moderate on where showers land, low on impact. The HRRR has moved its biggest cell between runs all evening (Friday dawn, then gone, now Saturday afternoon), which is typical of scattered showers in cold, unstable air: any one street can get a heavy 15 minutes or nothing. Every model's Friday-morning number is far below the Yellow line, and the RRFS's biggest hour, 0.15 in, would need to nearly triple to trip the 0.40 in burst alarm. The wildcard remains a brief thunderstorm (NWS: 10%) on wet ground near the morning high tide. Most likely outcome: wet streets and full gutters, no flooding.

sections.title: What to do
sections.text:
• No need to move cars out of the cul-de-sac.
• A glance at the dashboard between 6 and 10 AM Friday is enough. If the 1-hour burst alarm trips (0.40 in in one hour), move cars and watch the street drain grates.
• Use Friday afternoon or Monday's dry spell to clear leaves from street drain grates and yard drains and check sandbags: Tuesday and Wednesday bring heavier rain with the king tides.
• If water does reach the sidewalk, a timestamped photo at the peak helps tune the dashboard.
• Cold mornings Friday and Saturday. Don't drive or walk through moving water.
